label: L17
title: Non-linear optimization modeling
brief: Non-linear optimization (NLO) covers problems with a non-linear objective and/or non-linear constraints, and the right algorithm depends on structure: constrained or not, convex or not. The lecture builds intuition through formulations: norm-based approximation $\min\{\|Ax-b\|: x\in X\}$ (least squares, minimax, absolute residuals), weighted/regularized linear and logistic regression, signal denoising, projection and the maximum inscribed ellipsoid, mean-variance portfolio optimization, Fermat-Weber and ball-circumscription facility location, floor planning, and ride-sharing pickup coordination. It then defines the general NLO, the classes QP, QCQP, SOCP, SDP and NLP, and local versus global minima. Convexity is the dividing line: convex sets and functions, operations that preserve convexity, and the first-order (tangent plane underestimates $f$) and second-order (Hessian PSD) tests. A convex optimization problem (convex objective minimized, convex inequality constraints, linear equalities) has a convex feasible region and every local minimum is global, which is why convex problems are solved efficiently while non-convex ones are much harder.
kp: NLO = non-linear objective and/or constraints; algorithm design depends on whether the problem is constrained and whether it is convex.
Approximation problem $\min\{\|Ax-b\|: x\in X\}$: squared $\ell_2$ gives least squares, $\ell_\infty$ gives minimax, $\ell_1$ gives absolute-residual fitting.
Regularized regression adds $\lambda R(\beta)$, e.g. $R(\beta)=\sum_j\beta_j^2$; weights $w_i$ shrink the influence of less important points (outliers).
Logistic regression maximizes the log-likelihood $\sum_i y_i\beta^\top x_i-\sum_i\log(1+e^{\beta^\top x_i})$, plus a regularization term.
Mean-variance portfolio: minimize $x^\top\Sigma x$ s.t. budget, expected return $\ge\beta$, no short sales; only the objective is non-linear, and it is convex because $\Sigma\succeq0$.
Fermat-Weber minimizes total weighted distance $\sum_iw_i\|x-c_i\|$; ball circumscription minimizes the maximum distance via an epigraph variable $\Delta$. Both are convex.
NLO classes: QP (convex iff $Q\succeq0$), QCQP, SOCP, SDP, general NLP.
Convexity is preserved by non-negative weighted sums, affine pre-composition, pointwise max, convex non-decreasing $h$ of convex $g$; every norm is convex.
First-order test: $f$ convex iff $f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)$; second-order test: iff $H(x)\succeq0$ everywhere. Quadratic $\tfrac12x^\top Px+q^\top x+r$ is convex iff $P\succeq0$.
Convex optimization: convex objective (min), convex $g_i(x)\le0$, linear $Ax=b$ give a convex feasible set, and every local minimum is global.

topics.x: Many NLOs minimize a norm of a residual, $\min\{\|Ax-b\|: x\in X\}$, and the norm sets the model: squared $\ell_2$ is least squares, $\ell_\infty$ is minimax, $\ell_1$ is absolute residuals. Weighted/regularized linear regression, regularized logistic regression, signal denoising with a jump penalty, projection onto a set, distance between two sets and the maximum inscribed ellipsoid are all instances.

Mean-variance portfolio optimization minimizes portfolio variance subject to a budget, an expected-return target and no short sales. Fermat-Weber places a facility to minimize total weighted distance; ball circumscription minimizes worst-case distance. Floor planning (bilinear area and norm distance constraints) and vehicle-customer pickup coordination (norm travel and walking times) add non-linearities to otherwise linear models.

topics.n: The general NLO and its classes
topics.x: NLO: minimize continuous $f$ subject to $g_i(x)\le0$ and $h_j(x)=0$, with feasible region $F$. Named classes are QP, QCQP, SOCP, SDP and general NLP. A local minimum is no worse than every feasible point in some ball $B(x,\varepsilon)$; a global minimum is no worse than every feasible point.

$S$ is convex if it contains the segment between any two of its points; intersections of convex sets are convex. $f$ is convex if it lies below its chords and concave if it lies above them. Non-negative weighted sums, affine pre-composition, pointwise maxima and convex non-decreasing outer functions preserve convexity, and every norm is convex.

topics.n: Recognizing convexity: first- and second-order tests
topics.x: The gradient gives the first-order Taylor approximation and the Hessian the second-order one. A differentiable $f$ is convex iff its tangent plane underestimates it everywhere, which turns local information into global information. A twice continuously differentiable $f$ is convex iff $H(x)\succeq0$ for all $x$; for a quadratic this means $P\succeq0$ (all eigenvalues non-negative).

A convex optimization problem minimizes a convex objective under convex inequality constraints and linear equalities, so its feasible region is convex. LP, Fermat-Weber, ball circumscription, convex quadratically constrained problems and mean-variance portfolio are convex. On a convex set with a convex objective every local minimum is global, which is why convex problems are tractable; some convex classes are easier than others, and non-convex problems are much harder.

cards.f: Approximation problem: general form and the three norm choices.
cards.b: $\min_x\{\|Ax-b\|: x\in X\}$. Least squares: $\sum_i(a_i^\top x-b_i)^2$. Minimax: $\max_i|a_i^\top x-b_i|$. Absolute residuals: $\sum_i|a_i^\top x-b_i|$.
cards.x: The model $Ax$ is linear; the non-linearity comes from the norm.

cards.f: Weighted and regularized linear regression objective.
cards.b: $\min_\beta\sum_i w_i\big(y_i-\sum_j x_{ij}\beta_j\big)^2+\lambda R(\beta)$, e.g. quadratic penalty $R(\beta)=\sum_j\beta_j^2$.
cards.x: $w_i$ down-weights less important points (outliers); $\lambda$ trades fit for well-behaved coefficients.

cards.f: Logistic regression: model and what is optimized.
cards.b: $p_i=\dfrac{e^{\beta^\top x_i}}{1+e^{\beta^\top x_i}}$. Maximize the log-likelihood $\sum_i[\log p_i\,1(y_i=1)+\log(1-p_i)\,1(y_i=0)]=\sum_i y_i\beta^\top x_i-\sum_i\log(1+e^{\beta^\top x_i})$, plus a regularization term.
$\min_x\|x-b\|^2+\lambda\sum_i(x_i-x_{i+1})^2$: stay close to the observations while penalizing jumps between neighbours.
cards.x: $\lambda=0$ returns $x=b$; large $\lambda$ forces a smooth signal.
$d$ is the centre, $D$ the shape; growing $\log|\det D|$ inflates the ellipsoid inside polytope $P$.

cards.b: $\min\ x^\top\Sigma x=\sum_i x_i^2\mathrm{Var}(r_i)+\sum_{i\ne j}x_ix_j\sigma_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_ix_i\le B$, $\sum_i\mu_ix_i\ge\beta$, $x\ge0$.
cards.x: Constraints are linear; only the risk objective is non-linear, and it is convex because $\Sigma\succeq0$.

cards.b: Fermat-Weber: $\min_x\sum_iw_i\|x-c_i\|$ s.t. $Ax\le b$ (total weighted distance). Ball circumscription: $\min\Delta$ s.t. $\|x-c_i\|\le\Delta\ \forall i$, $Ax\le b$ (maximum distance).
cards.x: Sum vs max of distances; both are convex optimization problems.

cards.f: Floor planning: which constraints are non-linear?
cards.b: Minimum area $w_ih_i\ge A_i$ (bilinear) and distance limits $\|(u_i,v_i)-(u_j,v_j)\|\le D_{ij}$ (norm). Containment, relative positioning $x_i+w_i+\rho\le x_j$ and the objective $2(W+H)$ are linear.
cards.x: Aspect-ratio bounds $l_i\le h_i/w_i\le u_i$ look non-linear but become linear after multiplying by $w_i>0$.

cards.b: Minimize arrival time $v_{n+1}$ s.t. $v_i\ge v_{i-1}+\|M_i-M_{i-1}\|/S$ (vehicle travel), $v_i\ge\|M_i-H_i\|/S_i$ (customer walks there first), $\|M_i-H_i\|\le W_i$ (max walk), $M_0=O$, $M_{n+1}=D$.
cards.x: Pickup locations $M_i$ are decisions, so distances are norms of decision variables.

cards.b: QP: $\min x^\top Qx+c^\top x$, $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$ (convex if $Q\succeq0$). QCQP: quadratic objective and constraints. SOCP: $\min c_0^\top x$ s.t. $\|Q_ix+p_i\|_2\le s_i^\top x+r_i$. SDP: $\min\langle C,X\rangle$ s.t. $\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i$, $X\succeq0$. NLP: general $f,g_i,h_j$.
cards.x: Each class is a special case of the general NLO.

cards.b: Local: $f(x)\le f(y)$ for all $y\in B(x,\varepsilon)\cap F$, for some $\varepsilon>0$. Global: $f(x)\le f(y)$ for all $y\in F$.
cards.x: Every global minimum is local; the converse needs convexity.

cards.b: $\alpha f_1+\beta f_2$ with $\alpha,\beta\ge0$; $f(Ay+b)$; $\max\{f_1,\dots,f_n\}$; $h(g(x))$ with $h$ convex non-decreasing and $g$ convex; any norm $\|x\|$.
cards.x: Negative coefficients or a non-monotone outer function break the guarantee.

cards.b: A differentiable $f$ is convex iff $f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)$ for all $x,y$.
cards.x: The tangent plane is a global underestimator: local information gives global information.

cards.b: A $C^2$ function is convex iff $H(x)\succeq0$ for all $x$. For $f=\tfrac12x^\top Px+q^\top x+r$: $\nabla f=Px+q$, $H=P$, so $f$ is convex iff $P\succeq0$ (all eigenvalues $\ge0$).
cards.x: Positive entries or a positive diagonal do not imply PSD; check eigenvalues or $u^\top Pu\ge0$.

cards.f: The three features of a convex optimization problem.
cards.b: A convex objective to be minimized, convex inequality constraints $g_i(x)\le0$, linear equality constraints $Ax=b$. Then the feasible region $F$ is convex.
cards.x: Maximizing a convex function or a non-linear equality like $x_1^2+x_2^2=1$ breaks convexity.

cards.f: Why is every local minimum of a convex problem global? (proof idea)
cards.b: Suppose $y\in F$ with $f(y)<f(x^*)$. For $\theta\in(0,1)$, $\theta x^*+(1-\theta)y\in F$ (convex $F$) and $f(\theta x^*+(1-\theta)y)<f(x^*)$ (convex $f$). As $\theta\to1$ these points enter every ball around $x^*$, contradicting local optimality.
cards.x: Convexity of $f$ gives the lower value; convexity of $F$ gives feasibility.

quiz.q: In the approximation problem $\min\|Ax-b\|$, which choice gives the minimax approximation?
quiz.e: Minimax minimizes the largest residual, which is the $\ell_\infty$ norm. The $\ell_1$ sum is the absolute-residual approximation, a different model.

quiz.q: A candidate $x$ has residuals $Ax-b=(3,-1,2)$. What are its least-squares, minimax and absolute-residual objective values?
quiz.e: Least squares $9+1+4=14$; minimax $\max\{3,1,2\}=3$; absolute residuals $3+1+2=6$. The tempting 4 sums the signed residuals and forgets the absolute value.

quiz.q: In the denoising model $\min_x\|x-b\|^2+\lambda\sum_i(x_i-x_{i+1})^2$, what does the solution approach as $\lambda\to0$?
quiz.e: With no jump penalty only $\|x-b\|^2$ remains, minimized at $x=b$. A constant signal is the opposite limit, $\lambda\to\infty$, where any jump is prohibitively costly.

quiz.q: Which part of the mean-variance portfolio model is non-linear?
quiz.e: The variance $x^\top\Sigma x$ is quadratic in $x$. Budget $\sum_ix_i\le B$ and return $\sum_i\mu_ix_i\ge\beta$ are linear even though $\mu_i$ are estimated.

quiz.q: Two stocks have $\mathrm{Var}(r_1)=4$, $\mathrm{Var}(r_2)=9$, $\mathrm{Cov}(r_1,r_2)=-2$. What is the variance of the portfolio $x=(1,1)$?
quiz.e: $x^\top\Sigma x=x_1^2\sigma_{11}+x_2^2\sigma_{22}+2x_1x_2\sigma_{12}=4+9-4=9$. 13 ignores the covariance; 11 counts the cross term only once.

quiz.q: How does the ball circumscription model express 'minimize the maximum distance to the demand nodes'?
o: Minimize $\sum_i\|x-c_i\|^2$, which equals the maximum distance
Fix $x$ at the weighted centroid of the $c_i$
quiz.e: $\Delta$ upper-bounds every distance, so minimizing it minimizes the maximum (epigraph form). The weighted sum is the Fermat-Weber objective, which optimizes total rather than worst-case distance.

quiz.q: In the vehicle-customer coordination model, what does $v_i\ge\|M_i-H_i\|/S_i$ enforce?
o: The vehicle reaches stop $i$ no earlier than customer $i$ can walk there
The vehicle drives at speed $S$ between stops
Stops are visited in index order
quiz.e: $\|M_i-H_i\|/S_i$ is customer $i$'s walking time to the pickup point, so the pickup time must be at least that. The walking limit is the separate constraint $\|M_i-H_i\|\le W_i$.

quiz.q: In the floor-planning model, which constraint stays non-linear in $(x_i,y_i,w_i,h_i,W,H)$ even after algebraic rearrangement?
quiz.e: The area constraint multiplies two decisions (bilinear). The tempting aspect-ratio bound becomes linear, $l_iw_i\le h_i\le u_iw_i$, after multiplying through by $w_i>0$.

quiz.q: Which class has a linear objective, linear equalities and constraints $\|Q_ix+p_i\|_2\le s_i^\top x+r_i$?
quiz.e: Norm $\le$ affine is a second-order cone constraint. SDP constrains a matrix variable $X\succeq0$; QCQP has quadratic forms, not norms.

quiz.q: Which statement about minima of a general NLO is always true?
o: Every global minimum is a local minimum
Every local minimum is a global minimum
There is at most one local minimum
Local minima only exist for unconstrained problems
quiz.e: A global minimum beats all feasible points, hence those in any ball. The converse requires convexity (the lecture's theorem), so it fails for general NLOs.

quiz.q: Given convex $f_1,f_2$, which function is NOT guaranteed convex by the lecture's propositions?
quiz.e: Only non-negative combinations preserve convexity; a difference has coefficient $-1$ (e.g. $0-x^2$ is concave). Max and affine pre-composition are both on the list.

quiz.q: Using the composition rule, which function is convex on $\mathbb R^n$?
quiz.e: $h=\exp$ is convex and non-decreasing and $g=\|x\|_2$ is convex, so $h(g(x))$ is convex. $\log(1+\cdot)$ and $\sqrt{\cdot}$ are non-decreasing but concave, so the rule does not apply (in 1D, $\sqrt{|x|}$ violates the chord inequality).

quiz.q: A differentiable $f$ satisfies $f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)$ for all $x,y$. What follows?
quiz.e: This is the first-order characterization of convexity (an iff). It does not give uniqueness: a constant function satisfies it and every point minimizes it.

o: No: $P$ has eigenvalue $-1$, so it is not PSD
Yes: all entries of $P$ are positive
Yes: the diagonal of $P$ is positive
quiz.e: $H=P$ with eigenvalues $2\pm3=5,-1$. Positive entries do not imply PSD: $u=(1,-1)$ gives $u^\top Pu=2-6+2=-2<0$.

quiz.q: What is the Hessian of $f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+x_1x_2+x_2^2$, and is $f$ convex?
quiz.e: $\partial^2f/\partial x_1^2=2$, $\partial^2f/\partial x_1\partial x_2=1$, $\partial^2f/\partial x_2^2=2$; eigenvalues $2\pm1$ are positive, so $H\succeq0$ everywhere. Off-diagonal entries alone say nothing about PSD.

quiz.q: Which is one of the three defining features of a convex optimization problem?
o: The objective is concave and minimized
quiz.e: Convex objective (minimized), convex $g_i(x)\le0$, and linear $Ax=b$. A concave objective is convex only when maximized.

quiz.q: Which problem is NOT a convex optimization problem in the lecture's sense?
o: $\min x^\top\Sigma x$ s.t. $\mathbf 1^\top x\le B$, $\mu^\top x\ge\beta$, $x\ge0$, with $\Sigma\succeq0$
quiz.e: Equalities must be linear; the circle $x_1^2+x_2^2=1$ is not convex (the midpoint of $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$ is the origin, off the circle). The other three are the lecture's convex examples.

quiz.q: In the proof that local minima of convex problems are global, what is the convexity of $F$ used for?
o: To guarantee $\theta x^*+(1-\theta)y$ is feasible, giving better feasible points arbitrarily close to $x^*$
To make the Hessian at $x^*$ PSD
To make the optimal solution unique
quiz.e: Convexity of $f$ gives the strictly lower value on the segment; convexity of $F$ makes those points feasible. Differentiability is never used in the argument.

written.q: A utility must site one facility $x\in\mathbb R^n$ to serve $m$ demand nodes at $c_i$ with demands $w_i\ge0$; feasible sites are $Ax\le b$. (a) Formulate the Fermat-Weber and ball-circumscription problems and explain what each optimizes. (b) Using the lecture's convexity rules, prove that both are convex optimization problems. (c) What does convexity buy you when you solve them?
written.m: (a) Fermat-Weber: $\min_x\sum_iw_i\|x-c_i\|$ s.t. $Ax\le b$, minimizing total weighted distance. Ball circumscription: $\min_{x,\Delta}\Delta$ s.t. $\|x-c_i\|\le\Delta$ for all $i$, $Ax\le b$, minimizing the maximum distance to any node (epigraph form of $\min\max_i\|x-c_i\|$). (b) A norm is convex and composing with the affine map $x\mapsto x-c_i$ preserves convexity, so each $\|x-c_i\|$ is convex; a non-negative weighted sum of convex functions is convex, so the Fermat-Weber objective is convex, and $Ax\le b$ is linear. For ball circumscription the objective $\Delta$ is linear, each constraint $\|x-c_i\|-\Delta\le0$ is a convex function $\le0$, and $Ax\le b$ is linear. Both have convex objective (minimized), convex inequalities and no non-linear equalities. (c) The feasible region is convex and every local minimum is global, so a local method that stops at a local optimum has found the best site.
k: Correct Fermat-Weber formulation (weighted sum of norms)
Correct ball-circumscription formulation with epigraph variable $\Delta$
Interprets sum vs max of distances

written.q: Let $f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Px+q^\top x+r$ with $P$ symmetric. (a) Give $\nabla f$ and the Hessian. (b) State the first- and second-order characterizations of convexity and derive the condition on $P$. (c) Decide convexity for $P_1=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$. (d) Show that, when $f$ is convex, any $x^*$ with $\nabla f(x^*)=0$ is a global minimizer.
written.m: (a) $\nabla f(x)=Px+q$, $H(x)=P$. (b) First-order: differentiable $f$ is convex iff $f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)$ for all $x,y$. Second-order: $C^2$ $f$ is convex iff $H(x)\succeq0$ for all $x$; here $H=P$ is constant, so $f$ is convex iff $P\succeq0$ ($u^\top Pu\ge0$ for all $u$, equivalently all eigenvalues $\ge0$). (c) $P_1$: trace 5, determinant $4-4=0$, eigenvalues 5 and 0, so PSD and $f$ is convex (not strictly). $P_2$: trace 2, determinant $1-4=-3$, eigenvalues 3 and $-1$, not PSD; $u=(1,-1)$ gives $u^\top P_2u=1-4+1=-2<0$, so $f$ is not convex. (d) Plug $x=x^*$ into the first-order condition: $f(y)\ge f(x^*)+0^\top(y-x^*)=f(x^*)$ for every $y$, so $x^*$ is a global minimizer.
k: States the second-order condition and concludes $P\succeq0$
Uses the first-order condition with zero gradient for global optimality
